title: Dirae. Pyra. Mors Didonis
titleEn: Dido's Curse, the Pyre and Her Death — Aeneid IV.607–705
part: Dido's Curse, the Pyre and Her Death (IV.607–705)
about: Dido's speech, begun in the previous part, reaches its end: she calls on the Sun, Juno, Hecate, the Furies and the gods of dying Elissa, and prays that Aeneas, if he must reach Italy, may be harried by war, torn from his son, forced into an unequal peace and die unburied. She charges the Tyrians to hate his race for ever, and calls on some unknown avenger to rise from her bones; she prays for shore to face shore, wave wave and arms arms. Then she looks for the quickest way to end her life. She sends the old nurse Barce for Anna, with the offerings, on the pretext of a rite to Stygian Jove that will burn the Trojan's pyre. Wild and pale, Dido bursts into the inner court, climbs the pyre, draws the Trojan sword, and, looking at the clothes and the bed, lies down and speaks her last words: she says that her life is done and her road travelled, that she founded a city and avenged her husband; she would have been happy had the Trojan ships never touched her shore. She will die, and let the cruel Trojan see the fire from the sea. Her women see her fallen on the blade, and an outcry runs through the palace and the city as if Carthage or Tyre were falling. Anna rushes through the crowd, tearing her face, and reproaches her sister: this is what the pyre was for; she should have been called to die too; she has destroyed them both and the whole city. She climbs the pyre, holds the dying woman, tries to wipe away the blood and catch the last breath. Three times Dido tries to rise, three times falls back, and groans at the sight of the daylight. Juno, moved by the length of her suffering and the hardness of her going, sends Iris down; because Dido is dying neither by fate nor by desert, Proserpina has not yet cut the golden lock that consecrates her to the underworld. Iris, on her saffron wings and trailing the colours of the rainbow, stands over her, cuts the lock in the name of Dis and releases her. The warmth slips away and the life passes into the winds. Book IV ends.

sentences.t:
Sol, qui terrarum flammis opera omnia lustras,
tuque harum interpres curarum et conscia Iuno,
nocturnisque Hecate triviis ululata per urbes,
et Dirae ultrices, et di morientis Elissae,
accipite haec, meritumque malis advertite numen,
sentences.l:
Sun, you who with flames of the lands all works survey,
and you, of these cares interpreter and aware, Juno,
and Hecate, howled to at night at crossroads through cities,
and avenging Furies, and gods of dying Elissa,
receive these things, and the deserved to ills turn your divinity,
sentences.i: Sun, who range with your fire over every work of the earth; Juno, who understand these cares and know them well; Hecate, whose name is howled at night where three roads meet in the cities; avenging Furies, and you gods of dying Elissa: take in these words, and turn your due power to my sufferings,
sentences.n: Dido's speech, which began at 590 in the previous part, runs on, at a new paragraph. It is a string of invocations (vocatives, no verb until 'accipite'). 'qui… lustras' is a relative clause, 'you who survey'; 'terrarum flammis opera omnia' has 'flammis' as ablative of means ('with your flames') and 'terrarum' as the genitive plural of 'terra', 'the works of the lands'. 'interpres' and 'conscia' are vocatives in apposition to Iuno, 'interpreter and sharer in these cares'. 'nocturnis… triviis' is an ablative of place, 'at night, at the crossroads', where Hecate was worshipped; 'ululata' is a perfect passive participle, 'howled to' (a transitive use of 'ululo'). 'Dirae ultrices' are the Furies; 'di' is the contracted nominative plural of 'deus'. 'accipite… advertite' are imperatives; 'malis' is a dative, 'to my ills', and 'meritum numen' means 'your due divine power'.

sentences.t: et nostras audite preces.
sentences.l: and our hear prayers.
sentences.i: and listen to my prayers.
sentences.n: 'audite' is another imperative. 'nostras… preces' is a plural of the speaker for 'my' (Dido regularly says 'nostro', 'nostris' of herself in this speech: you will see it again at 623, 625, 662). 'et' begins the sentence by joining it to the invocation.

sentences.t:
Si tangere portus
infandum caput ac terris adnare necesse est,
et sic fata Iovis poscunt, hic terminus haeret:
sentences.l:
If to touch ports
the unspeakable head and to lands to sail is necessary,
and thus the fates of Jove demand, here the limit sticks:
sentences.i: If that unspeakable creature must reach harbour and sail up to the land, and if the fates of Jupiter so demand and this limit stands fixed:
sentences.n: 'Si… necesse est' is a condition ('if it is necessary'), and its subjects are the two infinitives 'tangere' and 'adnare'. 'infandum caput' is Aeneas: 'caput' (head) stands for the person, and 'infandum' means 'not to be spoken of', 'unspeakable'. 'terris' is a dative of direction with 'adnare' (a poetic use; prose would have 'ad terras'), 'to sail to land'. 'sic fata Iovis poscunt' means 'the fates of Jove demand it so', with 'Iovis' a genitive, and 'hic terminus haeret' 'this limit is fixed', the destined end of the voyage. The colon is followed by 'at', 'but even so', beginning the wishes that follow.

sentences.t:
at bello audacis populi vexatus et armis,
finibus extorris, complexu avulsus Iuli,
auxilium imploret, videatque indigna suorum
funera;
sentences.i: yet let him be harried by the war and weapons of a daring people, exiled from his own land, torn from the arms of Iulus; let him beg for help and see his own people die undeservedly;
sentences.n: 'imploret… videat' are present subjunctives of wish (or jussive), 'let him beg… let him see'; Aeneas, 'infandum caput', is still the subject. 'bello audacis populi vexatus et armis': 'bello' and 'armis' are ablatives of means with 'vexatus' ('harassed'), and 'audacis… populi' is a genitive singular (the -is ending is not an accusative plural here); the people are the Latins whose war fills the second half of the poem. 'finibus' is an ablative of separation with 'extorris' ('out of his land'), and so is 'complexu' with 'avulsus'. 'Iuli' is the genitive of Iulus (Ascanius). 'indigna… funera' means 'undeserved deaths', neuter plural, with 'suorum' a genitive plural, 'of his own'.

sentences.t:
nec, cum se sub leges pacis iniquae
tradiderit, regno aut optata luce fruatur,
sed cadat ante diem, mediaque inhumatus harena.
sentences.l:
nor, when himself under the terms of an unfair peace
he shall have surrendered, in kingdom or in longed-for light may he take joy,
but let him fall before his day, and in mid sand unburied.
sentences.i: and when he has put himself under the terms of an unequal peace, let him not enjoy his kingdom or the light he longs for, but fall before his time and lie unburied in the middle of the sand.
sentences.n: 'nec… fruatur' is a negative wish in the present subjunctive; 'fruor' takes the ablative, so 'regno aut optata luce' are ablatives ('enjoy his kingdom or the longed-for light'). 'cum se… tradiderit' has a perfect form that is either a future perfect indicative or a perfect subjunctive (the two coincide in the third person here), 'when he shall have given himself up'. 'iniquae' is a genitive singular, with 'pacis'. 'optata luce' is the light of life, so 'life he longs for'. 'cadat' is another wish; 'ante diem' means 'before his day', 'untimely'; 'inhumatus' ('unburied') is the worst fate in the ancient imagination, and 'media… harena' is an ablative of place, 'in the middle of the sand'.

sentences.t: Haec precor, hanc vocem extremam cum sanguine fundo.
sentences.l: These things I pray, this voice last with blood I pour.
sentences.i: This is my prayer, and this last cry I pour out with my blood.
sentences.n: 'precor' is a deponent verb, 'I pray'. 'hanc vocem extremam' means 'this last utterance'; 'fundo' is the verb 'pour out', and 'cum sanguine' links the words with her life-blood, which is about to flow.

sentences.t:
Tum vos, o Tyrii, stirpem et genus omne futurum
exercete odiis, cinerique haec mittite nostro
munera.
sentences.l:
Then you, O Tyrians, stock and race all future
harass with hatreds, and to our ashes these send
gifts.
sentences.i: Then you, men of Tyre, hound his stock and all the generations still to come with your hatred; let that be the offering you send to my ashes.
sentences.n: 'o Tyrii' is a vocative; the Carthaginians are Tyrian colonists. 'exercete' is an imperative of 'exerceo', 'keep busy, harry'; 'odiis' is an ablative of means. 'stirpem et genus omne futurum' has 'omne futurum' agreeing with 'genus', 'all the race that is to be'. 'cineri… nostro' is a dative ('to my ashes') with 'nostro' for 'meo'. 'haec… munera' frames the line break: the hatred of the Tyrians is the funeral offering.

sentences.t: Nullus amor populis, nec foedera sunto.
sentences.l: No love to the peoples, nor treaties let there be.
sentences.i: Let no affection pass between our nations, and no compact bind them.
sentences.n: 'sunto' is the future imperative (third person plural) of 'sum', a solemn legal form, 'let there be'; 'nullus amor populis' has 'populis' as a dative, 'between the peoples', and 'nec foedera' continues the prohibition. Roman readers heard here the origin of the long hostility between Rome and Carthage.

sentences.t:
Exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor,
qui face Dardanios ferroque sequare colonos,
nunc, olim, quocumque dabunt se tempore vires.
sentences.l:
Arise some one from my bones, an avenger,
who with torch Dardanians and with iron may pursue, settlers,
now, hereafter, at whatever time shall offer themselves the powers.
sentences.i: From my own bones let some avenger spring, to harry the Trojan settlers with brand and with blade, now, or later, whenever the strength is there.
sentences.n: 'exoriare' is a present subjunctive (a wish) of the deponent 'exorior', second person singular, addressed to 'aliquis' ('some one', unnamed); 'ultor' is a predicate noun, 'as avenger'. 'qui… sequare' is a relative clause of purpose, the subjunctive 'sequare' standing for 'sequaris' (the -re form of the second person); 'face… ferroque' are ablatives of means, 'with fire and sword'. 'Dardanios… colonos' are the Trojan settlers in Italy. 'quocumque dabunt se tempore vires' means 'whenever the strength offers itself'. Roman readers took the unnamed avenger to be Hannibal.

sentences.t:
Litora litoribus contraria, fluctibus undas
imprecor, arma armis; pugnent ipsique nepotesque.”
sentences.l:
Shores to shores opposed, to waves waves
I invoke as a curse, arms to arms; let them fight, themselves and their descendants.”
sentences.i: My curse is that coast should face coast in enmity, sea face sea, and weapon face weapon; and may they fight, themselves and their grandsons after them.”
sentences.n: 'imprecor' means 'I call down (as a curse)', and its objects are 'litora… contraria', 'undas' and 'arma', with the datives 'litoribus', 'fluctibus' and 'armis' (opposition, 'against'). 'Litora litoribus… arma armis' is the repeated sound-play of curse formulas. 'pugnent' is a jussive subjunctive, 'let them fight'; 'ipsi… nepotesque' means 'they and their descendants' ('nepotes' are grandsons, descendants). The closing mark ” ends the speech that began at 590 in the previous part.

sentences.t:
Haec ait, et partis animum versabat in omnis,
invisam quaerens quam primum abrumpere lucem.
sentences.l:
These things she says, and parts her mind was turning to all,
hated seeking as soon as possible to break off the light.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and turned her mind to every course, seeking the quickest way to break off the life she loathed.
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins here. 'ait' is the verb of speaking after the speech; 'partis… in omnis' has two accusative plurals in -is, 'in all directions'; 'versabat' is an imperfect, 'was turning over'. 'invisam… lucem' means 'the hated light', which stands for life ('lux' as the light of day); 'quam primum' means 'as soon as possible'; 'abrumpere' is an infinitive, 'to break off', depending on 'quaerens'.

sentences.t: Tum breviter Barcen nutricem adfata Sychaei;
sentences.l: Then briefly Barce the nurse she addressed of Sychaeus;
sentences.i: Then she spoke briefly to Barce, the nurse of Sychaeus;
sentences.n: 'adfata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'adfor' ('speak to'), used as a main verb (understand 'est'): deponent perfect participles have an active sense, and you will see this constantly (685, 686, 688 below). 'Barcen' is a Greek accusative; 'nutricem' is in apposition, and 'Sychaei' is the genitive of Sychaeus, Dido's dead husband, whose nurse she was.

sentences.t: namque suam patria antiqua cinis ater habebat:
sentences.l: for her own in country ancient ash black held:
sentences.i: for her own nurse lay in black ash in the old country:
sentences.n: 'namque' gives the reason for 'Sychaei': Dido's own nurse is dead. 'suam' stands for 'suam nutricem', 'her own (nurse)'; 'patria antiqua' is an ablative of place, 'in the old homeland' (Tyre), and 'cinis ater' is 'black ash', here a masculine noun, subject of 'habebat'. The colon opens the speech that follows.

sentences.t: “Annam cara mihi nutrix huc siste sororem;
sentences.l: “Anna — dear to me, nurse — here make stand, my sister;
sentences.i: “Nurse, dear to me, bring my sister Anna here;
sentences.n: Dido's speech to Barce opens with the mark “ and runs to 640. 'cara mihi nutrix' is a vocative, with 'mihi' a dative with 'cara'. 'Annam… sororem' is the accusative object, enclosing the vocative. 'siste' is an imperative of 'sisto' used transitively, 'make stand', so 'bring'. 'huc' means 'here'.

sentences.t:
dic corpus properet fluviali spargere lympha,
et pecudes secum et monstrata piacula ducat:
sentences.l:
say, let her hasten the body to sprinkle with river water,
and victims with her and the shown atonements let her lead:
sentences.i: tell her to hurry and sprinkle herself with water from the river, and to bring the beasts and the atoning offerings that have been prescribed:
sentences.n: 'dic properet' has 'ut' omitted: 'tell her (that) she is to hurry', a command idiom with 'dic' and 'fac'; 'properet' and 'ducat' are present subjunctives. 'corpus… spargere' means 'to sprinkle her body' (an infinitive depending on 'properet'); 'fluviali lympha' is an ablative of means, 'with river water', a rite of purification. 'pecudes… piacula' are the victims and the expiatory offerings, and 'monstrata' is a perfect passive participle, 'pointed out', 'prescribed' (by the priestess).

sentences.t: sic veniat;
sentences.l: thus let her come;
sentences.i: let her come so;
sentences.n: 'sic' means 'in this way' (purified and bringing the offerings); 'veniat' is a jussive subjunctive.

sentences.t: tuque ipsa pia tege tempora vitta.
sentences.l: and you yourself cover the temples with a holy fillet.
sentences.i: and bind your own brow, too, with a holy fillet.
sentences.n: 'ipsa' is feminine nominative, 'you yourself' (Barce); 'tege' is an imperative of 'tego'; 'tempora' (neuter plural, 'the temples of the head') is the object; 'pia… vitta' is an ablative of means, the sacred woollen band (vitta) worn at rites. Barce's own preparation helps keep the plan hidden.

sentences.t:
Sacra Iovi Stygio, quae rite incepta paravi,
perficere est animus, finemque imponere curis,
Dardaniique rogum capitis permittere flammae.”
sentences.l:
Rites to Jove of the Styx, which duly begun I have prepared,
to complete is my purpose, and an end to put to cares,
and the pyre of the Dardan head to give over to the flame.”
sentences.i: The rites to Stygian Jove that I began in due form and have made ready, I mean to finish, and to put an end to my cares, and to give the Trojan's funeral pyre to the flames.”
sentences.n: 'Sacra… quae… paravi' is the object of 'perficere', with the relative clause inside; 'Iovi Stygio' (dative) is Jupiter of the underworld, that is Dis or Pluto. 'rite incepta' means 'duly begun', a neuter plural participle agreeing with 'quae'. 'est animus' with infinitives means 'I intend', 'est mihi animus'; 'perficere… imponere… permittere' are the infinitives; 'curis' is a dative, 'to my cares'. 'Dardanii… capitis' means 'of the Dardanian head', 'caput' standing for Aeneas as at 613, and the pyre is to burn his effigy and arms (kept in 507–508). The mark ” closes the speech to Barce.

sentences.t: Sic ait:
sentences.l: Thus she says:
sentences.i: So she spoke.
sentences.n: 'Sic ait' is the formula that ends a speech (compare 630 and 704); 'ait' is a historic present. The colon sets the nurse's action against it.

sentences.t: illa gradum studio celerabat anili.
sentences.l: she her pace with zeal was quickening, an old woman's.
sentences.i: Barce quickened her step with all the eagerness an old woman has.
sentences.n: 'illa' is Barce; 'celerabat' is an imperfect, 'was hastening' (The Latin Library prints 'celebrabat', 'was crowding', which would give no clear sense with 'gradum'). 'studio… anili' is an ablative of manner, with 'anili' the adjective 'of an old woman' (from 'anus'), the nurse's age set against the speed her mistress wants.

sentences.t:
At trepida, et coeptis immanibus effera Dido,
sanguineam volvens aciem, maculisque trementis
interfusa genas, et pallida morte futura,
sentences.l:
But trembling, and by undertakings monstrous wild, Dido,
bloody rolling her eye, and with blotches trembling
spread over cheeks, and pale with death to come,
sentences.i: But Dido, shaken and wild with the monstrous thing she has begun, rolling a bloodshot eye, her trembling cheeks overspread with blotches, and pale at the death to come,
sentences.n: 'At' turns to Dido; 'trepida' is 'agitated'; 'coeptis immanibus' is an ablative of cause, 'at the monstrous things begun', with 'effera' ('wild'). 'sanguineam… aciem' means 'bloodshot gaze' ('acies' is the keen look of the eye); 'volvens' is a present participle. 'maculis… interfusa genas' has 'maculis' as an ablative of means ('with blotches') and 'interfusa' as a passive participle with an accusative of respect 'genas' ('overspread as to the cheeks'), the Greek-style accusative you saw at 518 ('exuta pedem'), 'trementis' being an accusative plural in -is agreeing with 'genas'. 'pallida morte futura' has a future participle with 'morte', 'pale at the death that is to come'.

sentences.t:
interiora domus inrumpit limina, et altos
conscendit furibunda rogos, ensemque recludit
Dardanium, non hos quaesitum munus in usus.
sentences.l:
the inner of the house she bursts into thresholds, and the high
she mounts, frenzied, pyre, and the sword she unsheathes
Dardan, not for these sought, a gift, uses.
sentences.i: she bursts into the inner courts of the house, climbs the high pyre in a frenzy, and draws the Trojan's sword, a gift that was not procured for such a use.
sentences.n: 'interiora… limina' means 'the inner thresholds', that is the inner part of the palace (Greenough spells the verb 'inrumpit'). 'altos… rogos' is a plural for a singular, 'the high pyre'; 'furibunda' is feminine nominative, 'raving'. 'ensem… Dardanium' is Aeneas's sword, left behind (507); 'munus' is in apposition, 'quaesitum' is a perfect passive participle agreeing with it, 'a gift not procured for these uses'; 'non hos… in usus' means 'not for these purposes'.

sentences.t:
Hic, postquam Iliacas vestes notumque cubile
conspexit, paulum lacrimis et mente morata,
sentences.l:
Here, after Ilian garments and the known couch
she saw, a little to tears and to thought having lingered,
sentences.i: There, when she saw the Trojan clothes and the familiar bed, she paused a little over her tears and her thoughts,
sentences.n: 'Hic' means 'here', on the pyre. 'postquam… conspexit' takes the perfect, 'after she saw'. 'Iliacas vestes notumque cubile' are the clothes (508) and the marriage bed they had shared; 'cubile' is a neuter noun. 'morata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'moror', 'having delayed', active in sense; 'lacrimis et mente' are ablatives, 'over her tears and thought' (cause). 'paulum' is an adverbial accusative, 'for a little'.

sentences.t: incubuitque toro, dixitque novissima verba:
sentences.l: and she fell upon the couch, and said the last words:
sentences.i: she fell on the couch, and spoke her last words:
sentences.n: 'incubuit' is the perfect of 'incumbo' with the dative 'toro', 'lay down upon the couch'; 'dixit' is the second verb of the pair, 'incubuitque… dixitque' being the double -que… -que ('both… and') you have seen before. 'novissima' is a superlative of 'novus' ('newest'), so 'last'.

sentences.t:
“Dulces exuviae, dum fata deusque sinebant,
accipite hanc animam, meque his exsolvite curis.
sentences.l:
“Sweet relics, while the fates and god allowed,
receive this spirit, and me from these release cares.
sentences.i: “Keepsakes I loved, while fate and heaven gave leave, take this spirit of mine into your keeping and loose me from these troubles.
sentences.n: A new paragraph; the speech opens with “ at 651 and ends at 658. 'exuviae' is a vocative plural: 'things taken off', here the clothes, sword and likeness of Aeneas. 'dum… sinebant' has the imperfect indicative plural with 'fata deusque' as the compound subject (The Latin Library has 'sinebat', singular, agreeing with 'deus' alone). 'deus' is the god who allowed her love, a vague word. 'animam' is 'breath, life'; 'exsolvite' is an imperative taking the ablative of separation, 'curis' ('from these cares').

sentences.t:
Vixi, et, quem dederat cursum fortuna, peregi,
et nunc magna mei sub terras ibit imago.
sentences.l:
I have lived, and, the course which fortune had given, I have completed,
and now great of me under the earth will go the shade.
sentences.i: My life is done; the road that fortune set me I have travelled to its end; and now a great shade of me will pass beneath the earth.
sentences.n: 'Vixi' is a perfect, 'I have lived', that is 'my life is over'. 'quem dederat cursum fortuna peregi' has the antecedent 'cursum' drawn into the relative clause; 'dederat' is a pluperfect, and 'peregi' means 'I have completed'. 'magna mei… imago' means 'a great shade of me': 'imago' is the shade or ghost of the dead, 'mei' the genitive of 'ego', and 'ibit' is a future; 'sub terras' is the accusative of motion.

sentences.t: Urbem praeclaram statui;
sentences.l: A city splendid I founded;
sentences.i: I founded a famous city;
sentences.n: 'statui' is a perfect, 'I established'; 'praeclaram' means 'very famous'. The three short clauses at 655–656 are linked without conjunctions (asyndeton), a list of her achievements.

sentences.t: mea moenia vidi;
sentences.l: my walls I saw;
sentences.i: I lived to see my own walls stand;
sentences.n: 'mea moenia vidi' has the neuter plural 'moenia', 'walls', and the perfect 'vidi'; the point is that she saw her work completed.

sentences.t: ulta virum, poenas inimico a fratre recepi;
sentences.l: having avenged my husband, penalties from an enemy from a brother I took back;
sentences.i: I avenged my husband, and took payment from my enemy of a brother;
sentences.n: 'ulta' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'ulciscor', 'having avenged', with an active sense; 'virum' is her husband Sychaeus. 'poenas… recepi' means 'I exacted punishment'; 'inimico a fratre' has the preposition set between the adjective and its noun, 'from my hostile brother' (Pygmalion, who killed Sychaeus: the story is in Book I).

sentences.t:
felix, heu nimium felix, si litora tantum
numquam Dardaniae tetigissent nostra carinae!”
sentences.l:
happy, alas too happy, if shores only
never Dardanian keels had touched ours!”
sentences.i: How blest I might have been, alas, beyond all measure, had Trojan ships never once touched our coast!”
sentences.n: 'felix, heu nimium felix' repeats the word for emphasis; the main verb is left to be supplied, 'I should have been'. 'si… tetigissent' is a pluperfect subjunctive, 'if they had touched', a condition contrary to fact; 'tantum' means 'only'. 'litora… nostra' enclose 'numquam Dardaniae tetigissent'; 'carinae' (keels) stands for ships. The mark ” closes the speech opened at 651.

sentences.t: Dixit, et, os impressa toro, “Moriemur inultae,”
sentences.l: She said, and, her face pressed to the couch, “We shall die unavenged,”
sentences.i: She spoke, and with her face pressed into the couch, “Unavenged I go to my death,”
sentences.n: New paragraph. 'os impressa' is the passive participle with an accusative of respect, 'pressed as to her face' (the Greek-style accusative again; compare 644). 'Moriemur inultae' means 'we shall die unavenged', 'inultae' being feminine plural for 'I', Dido speaking of herself in the plural. The speech marks that follow at 659–660 are misprinted; see the notes on the next two units.

sentences.t: “sed moriamur ait.
sentences.l: “but let us die,” she says.
sentences.i: “yet die I will,” she says.
sentences.n: The print has “ before 'sed' and nothing closing it before 'Sic, sic', a misprint for a closing ” after 'moriamur' (the sentence 'Moriemur inultae, sed moriamur' is Dido's, broken by 'ait'), corrected here in the English layers (the Latin keeps the print, since the checks require it to match the edition). 'moriamur' is a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us die'; 'ait' is an interrupting verb of saying.

sentences.t: Sic, sic iuvat ire sub umbras:
sentences.l: “Thus, thus it pleases to go under the shades:
sentences.i: “So, and so, I am glad to go down among the shades:
sentences.n: The print has no opening mark before 'Sic, sic', a misprint for “ (a new quotation begins after 'ait'), corrected here in the English layers (the Latin keeps the print). 'Sic, sic' is a doubled adverb, 'thus, thus', usually taken as the gesture or the stroke itself with the sword; 'iuvat' is an impersonal verb with an infinitive, 'it pleases (me) to go'. 'sub umbras' is the accusative of motion, 'to the shades below'.

sentences.t:
Hauriat hunc oculis ignem crudelis ab alto
Dardanus, et nostrae secum ferat omina mortis.”
sentences.l:
“Let him drink in this fire with his eyes, cruel, from the deep,
the Dardan, and of our death with him carry the omens.”
sentences.i: “Let the pitiless Trojan drink this fire in with his eyes from the open sea, and carry the omen of my death away with him.”
sentences.n: 'hauriat… ferat' are jussive subjunctives of wish. 'hunc ignem' is the fire of the pyre, which Aeneas will see burning as he sails away; 'oculis' is an ablative of means, and 'haurio' means 'draw up, drain', hence 'drink in'. 'ab alto' means 'from the deep sea'. 'crudelis… Dardanus' is a nominative, the adjective set at the end of one line and its noun at the start of the next. 'secum' is 'with him'; 'omina… mortis' means 'omens of death', and 'nostrae' is a plural for 'my'. The mark ” ends the speech (659–662).

sentences.t: Dixerat;
sentences.l: She had spoken;
sentences.i: She had finished;
sentences.n: 'Dixerat' is the pluperfect, 'she had spoken'; the epic formula that closes a speech (like 'Sic ait'), here followed at once by the result. The stroke itself is never narrated: it falls in the gap between 'Dixerat' and 'atque'.

sentences.t:
atque illam media inter talia ferro
conlapsam aspiciunt comites, ensemque cruore
spumantem, sparsasque manus.
sentences.l:
and her in the midst of such words by the iron
collapsed they see companions, and the sword with gore
foaming, and the spattered hands.
sentences.i: and in the midst of such words her attendants see her fallen on the blade, the sword foaming with blood, and her hands spattered.
sentences.n: 'illam… conlapsam' is an accusative with a perfect participle after 'aspiciunt' ('they see her collapsed'; Greenough spells 'conlapsam'). 'ferro' is an ablative, 'on the steel'. 'media inter talia' has the preposition set between the adjective and its noun, 'in the midst of such (words)'. 'comites' are her attendants; 'ensem… spumantem' has 'cruore' as an ablative of means ('foaming with gore'); 'sparsas manus' is another accusative with a participle, 'her hands sprinkled (with blood)'.

sentences.t:
It clamor ad alta
atria;
sentences.l:
Goes up an outcry to the high
halls;
sentences.i: A cry goes up to the lofty halls;
sentences.n: 'It' is the present of 'eo' ('goes'), not the English pronoun; 'clamor' is its subject. 'ad alta… atria' has the adjective set at the end of one line and its noun at the start of the next.

sentences.t: concussam bacchatur Fama per urbem.
sentences.l: shaken rages Rumour through the city.
sentences.i: and Rumour runs wild through the shaken city.
sentences.n: 'Fama' is personified Rumour (as in 173–197 earlier in this book); 'bacchatur' is a deponent, 'rages like a Bacchant'. 'concussam… urbem' means 'the shaken city', the participle set before the noun.

sentences.t:
Lamentis gemituque et femineo ululatu
tecta fremunt;
sentences.l:
With laments and groaning and womanly wailing
the roofs roar;
sentences.i: The roofs ring with lamenting, groaning and the wailing of women;
sentences.n: 'lamentis… gemituque et… ululatu' are ablatives of means in a string joined with -que… et; 'femineo' means 'of women'. 'tecta' (roofs) stands for the houses, and 'fremunt' is 'roar, resound'.

sentences.t:
resonat magnis plangoribus aether,
non aliter, quam si immissis ruat hostibus omnis
Karthago aut antiqua Tyros, flammaeque furentes
culmina perque hominum volvantur perque deorum.
sentences.l:
resounds with great beatings of the breast the sky,
not otherwise than if, enemies let in, were falling all
Carthage or ancient Tyre, and flames raging
roofs, and over of men may roll and over of gods.
sentences.i: The very sky echoes with the great beating of breasts, just as if all Carthage or ancient Tyre were falling to enemies let in, and raging flames were rolling over the rooftops of men and of gods.
sentences.n: 'aether' is a Greek nominative; 'plangoribus' is an ablative of means. 'non aliter quam si… ruat… volvantur' means 'not otherwise than if… were falling', the present subjunctive in a comparison ('as if'). 'immissis hostibus' is an ablative absolute. 'omnis Karthago' has 'omnis' as a nominative singular feminine agreeing with 'Karthago' (not the accusative plural in -is you have seen elsewhere); 'Tyros' is a Greek nominative; 'Karthago' is Greenough's spelling. 'culmina perque hominum volvantur perque deorum' has 'per' set after its noun 'culmina' (with -que between) and repeated, with 'culmina' understood again for 'deorum': 'over the roofs of men and (over the roofs) of gods', that is houses and temples.

sentences.t:
Audiit exanimis, trepidoque exterrita cursu
unguibus ora soror foedans et pectora pugnis
per medios ruit, ac morientem nomine clamat:
sentences.l:
Heard it breathless, and with trembling run terrified
with nails the face the sister disfiguring and the breast with fists
through the midst rushes, and the dying by name calls:
sentences.i: Her sister heard it, breathless with terror, and in a trembling, frightened rush, tearing her face with her nails and beating her breast with her fists, she burst through the crowd and called the dying woman by name:
sentences.n: New paragraph. 'Audiit' is the contracted perfect 'audivit'; 'exanimis' means 'breathless', and with 'exterrita' it agrees with 'soror' (Anna). 'trepido… cursu' is an ablative of manner; 'unguibus… pugnis' are ablatives of means, 'with nails… with fists'. 'ora… pectora' are plurals for singulars, a common poetic plural, and 'foedans' is a present participle, 'disfiguring'. 'per medios' means 'through the middle (of the crowd)'; 'ruit' is a historic present, 'rushes'. 'morientem' is a present participle, accusative, 'her who was dying'. The colon opens Anna's speech.

sentences.t: “Hoc illud, germana, fuit?
sentences.l: “This that, sister, was it?
sentences.i: “Was this what it meant, sister?
sentences.n: Anna's speech opens with the mark “ and runs to 684. 'germana' is a vocative, 'sister'. 'Hoc illud fuit?' is a question without a question word, 'was this that (thing)?', that is 'was this what the pyre was for'.

sentences.t: Me fraude petebas?
sentences.l: Me by deceit you were seeking?
sentences.i: Was it me you were deceiving?
sentences.n: 'me' comes first for emphasis; 'petebas' is an imperfect, 'were you aiming at', and 'fraude' is an ablative of means, 'by a trick'.

sentences.t: Hoc rogus iste mihi, hoc ignes araeque parabant?
sentences.l: This the pyre that to me, this the fires and altars were preparing?
sentences.i: Was this what that pyre of yours, those fires and altars, were making ready for me?
sentences.n: 'hoc… hoc' is an anaphora, 'this… this'; 'iste' has the force of 'that pyre of yours' (the second-person pronoun). 'mihi' is a dative of advantage. 'parabant' is plural with the three subjects 'rogus… ignes araeque'.

sentences.t: Quid primum deserta querar?
sentences.l: What first, deserted, shall I lament?
sentences.i: Forsaken, what shall I mourn first?
sentences.n: 'querar' is a deliberative subjunctive (first person), 'what am I to lament?'; 'deserta' is feminine nominative, 'abandoned'; 'primum' is an adverb, 'first'.

sentences.t:
Comitemne sororem
sprevisti moriens?
sentences.l:
A companion, your sister,
did you scorn, dying?
sentences.i: Did you, in dying, scorn your sister as a companion?
sentences.n: '-ne' is the enclitic question particle, attached to the emphatic word, 'comitem'. 'comitem' is a predicate accusative, 'as a companion'. 'sprevisti' is the ordinary second-person perfect, 'you scorned' (the contracted form to watch for is 'exstinxti' at 682); 'moriens' means 'while dying'.

sentences.t: Eadem me ad fata vocasses:
sentences.l: To the same me to fates you should have called:
sentences.i: You should have called me to the same fate:
sentences.n: 'vocasses' is the contracted pluperfect subjunctive 'vocavisses', a wish about the past, 'you should have called', 'would that you had'. 'eadem… fata' is a poetic plural for the singular. The colon introduces the explanation at 679.

sentences.t: idem ambas ferro dolor, atque eadem hora tulisset.
sentences.l: the same both with the sword grief, and the same hour would have carried off.
sentences.i: One grief should have carried us both off on the blade, in one hour.
sentences.n: 'tulisset' is a pluperfect subjunctive in the apodosis of the unreal wish ('would have taken'); 'ambas' is an accusative feminine plural, 'both of us'; 'ferro' is an ablative of means. 'dolor' and 'hora' are the subjects, the verb agreeing with the nearer; 'idem… dolor atque eadem hora' means 'the same grief and the same hour'.

sentences.t:
His etiam struxi manibus, patriosque vocavi
voce deos, sic te ut posita crudelis abessem?
sentences.l:
With these even I built hands, and ancestral I called
with voice gods, so that you laid down, cruel, I should be absent?
sentences.i: Did I build it with these very hands, and call on our fathers' gods with my own voice, only to be cruelly away when you were laid on it?
sentences.n: 'His… manibus' is an ablative, 'with these hands', and 'etiam' means 'even'; 'struxi' is the perfect of 'struo', 'I built' (the pyre). 'patrios… deos' means 'the gods of our fathers' (the gods of Tyre). 'sic… ut… abessem' is a result or purpose clause with the imperfect subjunctive, in an indignant question, 'so that I should be absent?'. 'te… posita' is an ablative absolute, 'you having been laid (on it)'. 'crudelis' is nominative feminine, Anna calling herself 'cruel'.

sentences.t:
Exstinxti te meque, soror, populumque patresque
Sidonios urbemque tuam.
sentences.l:
You have killed yourself and me, sister, and the people and fathers
Sidonian and the city yours.
sentences.i: Sister, you have destroyed yourself and me, your people and the Sidonian elders, and your own city.
sentences.n: 'Exstinxti' is the syncopated perfect 'exstinxisti', as Greenough spells it. 'te meque… populumque patresque… urbemque' is a polysyndeton, the objects heaped up with -que. 'soror' is a vocative. 'Sidonios' agrees with 'patres' (and means 'Phoenician'); 'patres' are the elders, the senate of Carthage. 'tuam' means 'your', the city being Dido's.

sentences.t:
Date volnera lymphis
abluam,
sentences.l:
Give: the wounds with waters
let me wash,
sentences.i: Grant it: let me bathe her wounds with water,
sentences.n: 'Date… abluam' has two verbs side by side with 'ut' left out and 'mihi' or 'veniam' understood, 'grant (it), let me wash'; 'abluam' is a present subjunctive of wish, with 'volnera' as its object. 'volnera' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulnera' (The Latin Library prints 'uulnera'); 'lymphis' is an ablative of means, 'with water'. Anna is speaking to the attendants.

sentences.t:
et, extremus si quis super halitus errat,
ore legam.
sentences.l:
and, last if any above breath wanders,
with mouth let me gather.”
sentences.i: and if any last breath still hovers over her, let me catch it with my lips.”
sentences.n: 'extremus… halitus' means 'the last breath'; 'si quis… errat' is a real condition with the indicative, 'if any… wanders', 'quis' standing for 'aliquis' after 'si'; 'super' is here an adverb, 'above', so 'still hovering over her'. 'ore' is an ablative, 'with the mouth'; 'legam' means 'let me gather up', a present subjunctive of wish (the nearest kin caught the last breath of the dying with a kiss). The closing mark ” of Anna's speech stands here, at the end of 'legam.'; the print has it at the head of the next unit (see that note).

sentences.t: ”Sic fata, gradus evaserat altos,
sentences.l: Thus having spoken, the steps she had climbed, the high,
sentences.i: Saying this, she had climbed the high steps,
sentences.n: The print has ” at the head of 'Sic fata', a misprint for a ” after 'legam.' at the end of the previous unit, corrected here in the English layers (the Latin keeps the print, since the checks require it to match the edition). 'Sic fata' is a perfect participle of the deponent 'for', 'having spoken', active in sense (as 'adfata' at 632). 'evaserat' is a pluperfect, 'she had gone up', with the accusative 'gradus… altos', 'the high steps' (of the pyre).

sentences.t:
semianimemque sinu germanam amplexa fovebat
cum gemitu, atque atros siccabat veste cruores.
sentences.l:
and half-living in lap sister embracing she was cherishing
with groan, and black she was drying with garment the blood.
sentences.i: and clasping her half-dead sister to her breast she held her, groaning, and dried the dark blood with her robe.
sentences.n: 'semianimem' is an accusative singular agreeing with 'germanam'; 'sinu' is an ablative, 'in her bosom'. 'amplexa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'amplector', 'having embraced' (active in sense, like 'fata' above); 'fovebat' is an imperfect, 'kept warm, cherished'. 'cum gemitu' means 'with a groan'; 'atros… cruores' is a plural for a singular, 'the dark blood'; 'veste' is an ablative of means, 'with her robe'; 'siccabat' means 'was drying'.

sentences.t:
Illa, graves oculos conata attollere, rursus
deficit;
sentences.l:
She, heavy eyes having tried to lift, again
fails;
sentences.i: She tries to lift her heavy eyes, and sinks again;
sentences.n: 'Illa' is Dido. 'conata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'conor', 'having tried', with an infinitive 'attollere', 'to lift', active in sense. 'graves oculos' is accusative plural (The Latin Library has 'grauis', no change of sense). 'deficit' is a present, 'fails, sinks back'; 'rursus' means 'again'.

sentences.t: infixum stridit sub pectore vulnus.
sentences.l: fixed hisses beneath the breast the wound.
sentences.i: and the wound, driven deep, hisses beneath her breast.
sentences.n: 'infixum… vulnus' means 'the wound that is fixed (in her)'; the participle agrees with 'vulnus'. Greenough spells it 'vulnus' here and 'volnera' at 683, and the spellings are kept as printed. 'stridit' means 'hisses' (breath and blood escaping the wound); 'sub pectore' is an ablative of place.

sentences.t: Ter sese attollens cubitoque adnixa levavit;
sentences.l: Three times herself lifting up and on elbow leaning she raised;
sentences.i: Three times she raised herself, propped on her elbow;
sentences.n: 'Ter' begins a three-fold repeated action, 'ter… ter' (690–691), with the ritual number three. 'sese attollens' means 'lifting herself up'; 'sese' is the reflexive object and also the object of 'levavit' (understood), 'she raised (herself)'. 'adnixa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'adnitor', 'leaning', active in sense; 'cubito' is an ablative, 'on her elbow'.

sentences.t:
ter revoluta toro est, oculisque errantibus alto
quaesivit caelo lucem, ingemuitque reperta.
sentences.l:
three times rolled back on the couch she was, and with eyes wandering in the high
she sought sky the light, and groaned at it found.
sentences.i: three times she fell back on the couch, and with wandering eyes she looked for the light in the high sky, and groaned when she found it.
sentences.n: 'revoluta… est' is a perfect passive, 'she was rolled back', 'she fell back'; 'toro' is an ablative (or dative) of the place, 'on the couch'. 'oculis errantibus' is an ablative of means, 'with wandering eyes'; 'alto… caelo' means 'in the high sky' (ablative of place, the adjective set apart). 'reperta' is a perfect passive participle, taken with 'lucem' ('the light, found'), 'groaned at finding it', the light she must now leave.

sentences.t:
Tum Iuno omnipotens, longum miserata dolorem
difficilisque obitus, Irim demisit Olympo,
quae luctantem animam nexosque resolveret artus.
sentences.l:
Then Juno omnipotent, having pitied the long grief
and the difficult death, Iris sent down from Olympus,
who the struggling spirit and the bound might release, limbs.
sentences.i: Then Juno, all-powerful, moved by the length of her suffering and the hardness of her going, sent Iris down from Olympus to loose the struggling spirit from the limbs that held it fast.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'omnipotens' is Juno's epithet (Juno, the goddess who had pursued the Trojans, here pities their victim; she was Dido's patron from the first book). 'miserata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'miseror', 'having pitied', active in sense; 'longum… dolorem difficilisque obitus' means 'the long pain and the hard death', with 'difficilis' an accusative plural in -is and 'obitus' an accusative plural of the fourth declension (a poetic plural for the singular). 'Irim' is a Greek accusative; Iris is the rainbow goddess and Juno's messenger. 'Olympo' is an ablative of separation without a preposition ('from Olympus'). 'quae… resolveret' is a relative clause of purpose, 'who was to release'; 'luctantem animam nexosque… artus' means 'the struggling spirit and the bound limbs', with 'artus' placed last.

sentences.t:
Nam quia nec fato, merita nec morte peribat,
sed misera ante diem, subitoque accensa furore,
sentences.l:
For because neither by fate, nor by deserved death she was perishing,
but wretched before day, and suddenly inflamed with madness,
sentences.i: For since she was perishing neither by fate nor by a death she had deserved, but a wretched woman before her time, kindled by a sudden frenzy,
sentences.n: 'Nam quia' means 'for since', giving the reason. 'nec fato, merita nec morte' has 'merita' agreeing with 'morte' and set before 'nec' ('nec merita morte'), 'neither by fate nor by a deserved death'; 'peribat' is an imperfect, 'was perishing'. 'misera ante diem' means 'wretched, before her day' (before her appointed time); 'accensa' is a perfect passive participle, 'kindled', and 'subito… furore' is an ablative of cause or means, 'by sudden madness'.

sentences.t:
nondum illi flavum Proserpina vertice crinem
abstulerat, Stygioque caput damnaverat Orco.
sentences.l:
not yet to her the yellow Proserpina from the crown the lock
had taken away, and to Stygian had she condemned the head, to Orcus.
sentences.i: Proserpina had not yet taken the golden lock from her head, nor given her life to the Stygian underworld.
sentences.n: 'nondum' means 'not yet'. 'illi' is a dative of reference ('from her'); 'flavum… crinem' is 'the golden lock'; 'vertice' is an ablative of separation, 'from the crown of her head'. The cutting of a lock from a victim's head consecrated it to the gods below, and here Proserpina is imagined as doing it for the dead. 'abstulerat… damnaverat' are pluperfects, 'had taken away… had condemned'; 'Stygio… Orco' is a dative, enclosing 'caput' (Orcus is another name of the underworld and its god).

sentences.t:
Ergo Iris croceis per caelum roscida pennis,
mille trahens varios adverso sole colores,
devolat, et supra caput adstitit:
sentences.l:
Therefore Iris with saffron through the sky dewy wings,
a thousand drawing various against sun colours,
flies down, and above the head stood:
sentences.i: So Iris, dew-bright on saffron wings, trailing a thousand shifting colours across the sun that faces her, flies down through the sky and stands above her head:
sentences.n: 'Ergo' means 'so, accordingly'; 'roscida' is 'dewy'; 'croceis… pennis' is an ablative of means, 'on saffron wings'. 'mille… colores' has the indeclinable 'mille', 'a thousand colours', and 'varios' means 'varied'; 'trahens' is a present participle, 'drawing (behind her)'. 'adverso sole' is an ablative absolute, 'with the sun opposite', as a rainbow forms. 'devolat' is a historic present and 'adstitit' a perfect (The Latin Library prints 'astitit', an orthographic variant); 'supra' takes the accusative 'caput'. The colon opens Iris's speech.

sentences.t:
“Hunc ego Diti
sacrum iussa fero, teque isto corpore solvo.”
sentences.l:
“This I to Dis
sacred, bidden, carry, and you from that body release.”
sentences.i: “On orders I take this lock away, hallowed to Dis, and loose you from that body.”
sentences.n: Iris's speech opens with “ at 702 and closes with ” here. 'Hunc' points forward to the lock she is about to cut ('crinem', 704) and is the object of 'fero', 'I take'. 'Diti' is the dative of 'Dis' (Pluto), 'to Dis'; 'sacrum' is a predicate adjective, 'as sacred, as consecrated'. 'iussa' is a perfect passive participle, 'having been ordered' (by Juno). 'teque… solvo' means 'and I release you'; 'isto corpore' is an ablative of separation, 'from that body of yours' ('iste' being the pronoun of the second person), matching 'resolveret' at 695.

sentences.t: Sic ait, et dextra crinem secat:
sentences.l: Thus she says, and with the right hand the lock she cuts:
sentences.i: So she speaks, and with her right hand cuts the lock;
sentences.n: 'Sic ait' is the formula as at 641; 'dextra' is an ablative of means with 'manu' understood, 'with the right (hand)'. 'crinem' is the lock of hair of 698; 'secat' is a historic present. The colon introduces the result.

sentences.t:
omnis et una
dilapsus calor, atque in ventos vita recessit.
sentences.l:
all and at once
slipped away the warmth, and into the winds life withdrew.
sentences.i: and all her warmth slipped away at once, and her life drew back and was gone into the winds.
sentences.n: 'omnis… calor' is a nominative singular masculine ('all the warmth'), not the accusative plural in -is you have seen elsewhere. 'et una' means 'and at once', 'together'. 'dilapsus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'dilabor', 'having slipped away', active in sense, with 'est' understood. 'in ventos' means 'into the winds'; 'vita' is the nominative, and 'recessit' a perfect, 'withdrew'. This is the last line of Book IV.
